object.description: Not the monster but the woman, at the moment she understands what she has become. Medusa's snakes are waking in her hair; her mouth is open, her brow knotted; she is turning, perhaps, to stone herself. Bernini carved it in the 1640s, in the years after his patron Urban VIII died and his own fortunes fell, and it has been read as a portrait of his disgrace. It is the only one of his works with a woman's face in pain that is not religious, and the Capitoline has had it since 1731. The scan is of the marble itself.
facts: The snakes were carved from the same block as the head, undercut so deeply that light passes behind them.
Bernini's own mistress, Costanza Bonarelli, whose bust he also carved, had her face slashed on his order in 1638.
It is displayed in the Capitoline Museums' Hall of the Geese.
